subject: botany_2

verification.note: Sourced from "Sr. Botany — My Baby Bullet-Q" (Sri Publishers, STAR-Q Pass Track), book p.31, printed question 35. Botany-II holds only ONE source book: the TSBIE Basic Learning Material in hand covers physics only, and no Telangana Botany-II board paper is in the corpus, so the two-book union check and the board back-test are BOTH structurally impossible for this card — "not checked" does NOT mean "checked and clean". Run both the moment a second source or a real paper arrives. The mark split is a claim until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it. BOOK ERROR, corrected on this card, and it has two faults in one printed line. The guide's F2 legend reads "1 CˢCˢ (spotted) : 2 CˢCᴰ (spotted & dotted) : 3 CᴰCᴰ (spotted & dotted)". The third class is ONE, not three — a 2x2 Punnett square cannot give a 1:2:3 — and CᴰCᴰ is DOTTED, not "spotted & dotted". The correct legend is 1 spotted : 2 spotted and dotted : 1 dotted.

insider_note: Co-dominance and incomplete dominance are the pair examiners set against each other. Co-dominance shows BOTH parent characters; incomplete dominance shows a NEW one in between. Say which is which.

page_header: Principles of Inheritance and Variation (Botany-II) · 4 marks

steps.label: What co-dominance is
steps.margin_note: Definition with the words 'both' and 'fully'. This is the contrast with the next question.
lines: CO-DOMINANCE is the condition in which BOTH
alleles of a pair are EQUALLY dominant.
In the heterozygote, both alleles express
themselves FULLY and INDEPENDENTLY.
Neither allele is dominant or recessive to the
other.
steps.why: Both alleles being expressed fully is what makes the heterozygote show two characters at once rather than one, or a blend.
common_mistakes: Saying co-dominance gives a blended character. That is INCOMPLETE dominance.
Saying one allele is partly dominant. In co-dominance BOTH are fully expressed.
steps.memory_tip: Both show, and both show completely.

steps.label: The lentil example
steps.margin_note: Give both examples if you have room. The blood group one is the strongest.
lines: Example 1: the ABO blood groups in humans.
The alleles I^A and I^B are co-dominant, so a
person carrying both has blood group AB.
Example 2: seed coat pattern in LENTIL plants.
A pure-breeding SPOTTED lentil (CˢCˢ) is crossed
with a pure-breeding DOTTED lentil (CᴰCᴰ).
steps.why: Blood group AB is the clearest case in the whole of genetics: the person is not intermediate between A and B but genuinely both.
common_mistakes: Naming no example. The question asks for one.
Giving snapdragon flower colour. That is INCOMPLETE dominance, not co-dominance.
steps.memory_tip: Blood group AB is both, not in between.

steps.label: The F1 generation
steps.margin_note: Say 'both, at the same time'. The word 'blend' must not appear.
lines: The F₁ heterozygotes (CˢCᴰ) are BOTH SPOTTED
AND DOTTED.
They show the phenotypic features of BOTH
parents at the same time.
Neither the spotted nor the dotted allele is
dominant or recessive to the other.
steps.why: The F1 carrying both patterns at once, rather than one of them or a mixture, is the observation that defines co-dominance.
common_mistakes: Saying the F1 is intermediate. It is not a blend; it shows BOTH patterns separately.
Saying the F1 resembles one parent. It resembles BOTH.
steps.memory_tip: Not in between, but both at once.

steps.label: The F2 ratio
steps.margin_note: All three classes with their genotypes and appearances, then the reason the ratios match.
lines: Selfing the F₁ gives:
1 CˢCˢ  spotted
2 CˢCᴰ  spotted AND dotted
1 CᴰCᴰ  dotted
The phenotypic and genotypic ratios are the
SAME, 1 : 2 : 1, because every genotype has its
own appearance.
steps.why: Because each of the three genotypes looks different, the two ratios cannot differ — which is the same reason incomplete dominance also gives 1:2:1.
common_mistakes: Writing the third class as 3. A 2 by 2 square gives 1:2:1, never 1:2:3. The guide misprints this.
Calling CᴰCᴰ 'spotted and dotted'. It is DOTTED — it carries no spotted allele.
Giving 3:1. That is the ratio for complete dominance.
steps.memory_tip: Three genotypes, three different looks, so 1:2:1 twice over.

steps.margin_note: No diagram mark. Draw it anyway on this question — the square is what protects you from the wrong ratio the guide prints.

steps.why: Setting the three F2 genotypes in a square shows immediately that there is one of the third class and not three, which is where the printed guide goes wrong.
common_mistakes: Drawing an F1 that looks like one parent. The F1 shows BOTH patterns.
Writing a 1:2:3 ratio under the square. Four boxes cannot give six offspring.
Marking the CᴰCᴰ box as spotted and dotted. It is DOTTED.
steps.memory_tip: Four boxes, so the classes must add to four: 1 + 2 + 1.
